children: The Alternative for Germany’s success in a state election probably won’t derail a recovery set to lift growth to 0.6% this year. But its anti-immigrant, pro-Russian stance could throttle longer-term attempts to tackle the country’s demographic, industrial and defence challenges.
Full view will be published shortly.
Follow Jon Sindreu on X and LinkedIn.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44% of the votes in the elections in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, according to exit polls. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) was a far second with around 17% of the votes. The AfD is now leading in German national opinion surveys as well, polling at 28% according to a recent INSA poll, compared with the CDU’s 20%.
